doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Teenage dance band The Nighthawks and its repertoire
summary: Aebersold bought stock arrangements at 15 and cut them down for The Nighthawks, playing standards; later pop requests and why he quit playing jobs.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: That is a question for a lot of us, and there are certain places in the country who do accept donations but sometimes it’s not as easy as it sounds. There’s a lot to consider about accepting a donation and into the future, what happens with it. If I could I’d like to take you back a little bit. You were born and playing early on in the mid-50s is that correct?
When you got in bands at that time can you remember what the songlist would have looked like? The repertoire?

Yes. “In the Mood,” “Tenderly,” “Pennsylvania 6-5000” songs like that. I sold my song — I bought arrangements when I was in high school. I was probably 15 years old and we started this little group called The Nighthawks. So I would buy those arrangements for a dollar and a quarter that had four trombones, five saxes, trumpets, you know. And we cut those down and played them with two saxes and one trumpet and piano, bass and drums and maybe a trombone if we were lucky, and maybe a tenor sax if the local band director’s son was free that day or that night. You know. But we started off playing what I now call the old standard from the Great American Songbook.
And they’ve lasted a long time. Were you playing for dancers? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Yes. Mainly dancers at the various animal clubs like The Moose and The Elks and The Lions. You know. Things like that. And then we played for sock hops at the high school. We played for various things but we played the same tunes kind of over and over, “Tuxedo Junction” comes to mind, “In the Mood,” “Satin Doll” I think.
Was there a point during this band’s life where pop music like early Elvis, Jerry Lee Lewis, started to creep in and did you get requests for such things?

I remember eventually playing “The Green Door,” “I Ain’t Nothin’ But a Hound Dog” and then a little later “Tie a Yellow Ribbon Around the Old Oak Tree” or something. Now that’s about it but I’ll tell you, in the early 90s I just stopped playing — I stopped playing any job where they were smoking, number one. And number two I think the band leader that I was playing with, bass at one time, we played together for some years but he was branching out into what you’re talking about and some country tunes and things. And he wanted to rehearse and I just said I can’t do this. So I think I quit on the same day that he fired me. And we were still good friends it’s just that that’s not what I wanted to spend my time doing. You know. So I quit doing that. No but it didn’t really infringe. That was in the 50s when we started so we made it way up into the 70s I think, still playing what we would now call standards.
